title: Function pointers: passing behaviour around
objective: By the end of this lesson you can declare and use a function pointer, recognise the pattern in real C libraries, and explain why this is where several exploitation techniques aim.

blocks.text: A function lives in memory and therefore has an address. A function pointer holds that address, which lets you decide at runtime which code to run. Every callback, every plugin system, and every dispatch table in C is built on this.

blocks.caption: Declaring one
lines: int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
int mul(int a, int b) { return a * b; }
int (*op)(int, int);      /* op is a pointer to a function taking (int,int) returning int */
op = add;                 /* the function name is its address */
printf("%d\n", op(2, 3)); /* 6 — same call site, different behaviour */

blocks.title: The parentheses are load-bearing
blocks.text: int (*op)(int, int) is a pointer to a function. int *op(int, int) is a function returning a pointer to int — a completely different thing. When the declaration gets hard to read, a typedef fixes it: typedef int (*BinaryOp)(int, int); then write BinaryOp op;

blocks.caption: qsort is the canonical example
lines: return (x > y) - (x < y);      /* -1, 0, or 1 without overflow */
/* qsort does not know what it is sorting. You supply the comparison. */

blocks.title: Do not write return x - y in a comparator
blocks.text: It looks neat and it overflows: with x = 2000000000 and y = -2000000000 the subtraction is undefined and the result may come out negative when it should be positive, silently producing a wrong sort order. (x > y) - (x < y) computes the same three-way result without any arithmetic that can overflow.

blocks.caption: An array of function pointers replaces a long switch
lines: for (size_t i = 0; i < sizeof commands / sizeof commands[0]; i++) {

blocks.text: Adding a command becomes adding a row to the table. This is how shells, interpreters, and device drivers organise their entry points — and when you read a driver's struct full of function pointers, you are reading exactly this pattern.

blocks.title: A function pointer in writable memory is a control-flow target
blocks.text: If an attacker can overwrite a function pointer — through a buffer overflow into a nearby struct, or a use-after-free where the freed object is reallocated with attacker data — then the next call through that pointer transfers control to an address they chose. This is why exploitation write-ups talk about vtables, hook tables, and callback fields, and why modern systems add mitigations such as control-flow integrity checks.

items: Mark tables of function pointers const when they never change — const data can be placed in read-only memory
Validate an index before using it to select from a dispatch table
Never build a function pointer from data that came from input
Treat a struct containing function pointers as a higher-value target when reviewing overflow risk nearby

blocks.caption: Work outward from the name
lines: taking (int, pointer to function taking int returning void)
returning a pointer to a function taking int returning void */

blocks.title: Build a small dispatch table
steps: Write add and mul, then int (*op)(int,int); assign each in turn and call through it
Add: typedef int (*BinaryOp)(int,int); and rewrite the declaration using it
Write compare_ints and sort an array with qsort
Change the comparator to return x - y and test it with INT_MAX and INT_MIN — observe the wrong order
Build the commands[] table above with two handlers and dispatch on argv[1]
Mark the table const and confirm it still compiles
Print the address of a function with printf("%p", (void *)add) and note it sits in the code region
blocks.expected: One call site producing different behaviour, a working qsort, a comparator that breaks on extreme values until you use the three-way form, and a dispatch table that replaces a switch. The address print shows the last piece: functions live in memory just like data.

cheatsheet: int (*op)(int,int) is a pointer to a function; int *op(int,int) is a function returning int *
A function name used as a value is its address
Call through it exactly like a normal call: op(2, 3)
typedef makes complicated function-pointer declarations readable
qsort takes a comparator — the standard callback pattern
Write (x > y) - (x < y), never x - y, in a comparator
An array of function pointers is a dispatch table and replaces a long switch
Mark constant tables const so they can live in read-only memory
Never derive a function pointer from input; validate any index used to select one

checkpoint.prompt: What is the difference between int (*f)(int) and int *f(int) ?

choices.C: The second is a function pointer array
choices.D: The first is a pointer to a function

checkpoint.explanation: The second is a function that returns a pointer to int. The parentheses bind the asterisk to the name rather than to the return type. A typedef removes the ambiguity for readers.

checkpoint.prompt: Why should a qsort comparator not return x - y ?
checkpoint.explanation: For large-magnitude values the subtraction is undefined and can produce the wrong sign — and therefore the wrong order. (x > y) - (x < y) produces the same three-way answer using only comparisons, so nothing can overflow.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is a writable function pointer a security-relevant target?

choices.B: Function pointers cannot be checked for NULL or validated in any way before the call
choices.D: Because an attacker who can overwrite it gains control of the next call through it

checkpoint.explanation: Via an overflow into a neighbouring struct or a use-after-free — the next call through it transfers control to an address they chose. This is why exploitation discussions focus on vtables, hook tables, and callback fields, and why const tables in read-only memory are a meaningful hardening step.

checkpoint.prompt: What does a dispatch table give you over a long switch statement?

choices.A: Type safety for the arguments of every handler
choices.C: Adding a case becomes adding a data row

checkpoint.explanation: The set of handlers becomes inspectable data rather than control flow. It is how shells, interpreters, and drivers organise entry points — the table is data you can read, extend, and mark const.
